items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Out-of-bounds access in _imagingmorph on a zero-width image
items.summary: SummaryA PPM or PGM file can declare a width of 0, which Pillow accepts, producing an image of size (0, N). Passing that image to ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() makes the native morphology code index a row buffer at outrow[width - 1], which is outrow[-1] when the width is 0. The process crashes.DetailsThe PPM parser reads width and height with no lower-bound check:src/PIL/PpmImagePlugin.py:119The native apply() writes the row edges with no guard that the width is positive:src/_imagingmorph.c:81 sets outrow[0] = outrow[width - 1] = 0;match() and get_on_pixels() use the same edge-indexing pattern.PoCfrom PIL import Image, ImageMorph# A width-0 image (also producible from a crafted PPM header). apply() indexes# outrow[width - 1] == outrow[-1] in native code.im = Image.new("L", (0, 5))ImageMorph.MorphOp(op_name="dilation4").apply(im)Run it:$ python 03_poc.pySegmentation fault (core dumped)Observed on a source build of commit 3e2ab96.Under AddressSanitizer:==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address (pc ... in apply)    #0 apply   src/_imagingmorph.c:81SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/_imagingmorph.c:81 in applyWith width 0 the outrow[width - 1] write lands on an unmapped page, so it surfaces as a SEGV pinned to the edge-write line rather than a redzone overflow.ImpactOut-of-bounds write in a C extension. Affects any application that runs a morphology operation on an image opened from untrusted input. Result is a crash and possible memory corruption.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-58r4-6rv3-gfh8https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112397https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/18f7c0dfee93063c51db6ed0ca8c4da2999dcb64https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-58r4-6rv3-gfh8

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS
items.summary: ============================================================================GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoSLocation: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:293  in GifImageFile._seek()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================A GIF of about 60 bytes can make Pillow allocate gigabytes of memory. This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption.The bug is in GifImageFile._seek() (src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to self._size and only then calls Image._decompression_bomb_check(). Nothing restores the old size when DecompressionBombError is raised, because seek() only rolls back on EOFError. After the caught error, im.size reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer im.im is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070.In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried seek(1) followed by load() then reaches load_prepare(), which calls Image.core.fill() with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...) and rotate(..., expand=True) also allocate from the stale size.The default paths are unaffected: plain Image.open() plus load(), ImageSequence.Iterator, and n_frames/is_animated. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order.DetailsGifImageFile._seek() lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs thedecompression-bomb check for the new size only after storing it on the object:# src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294  (GifImageFile._seek)x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2)x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6)if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image:    self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1])   # state mutated    Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size)                 # ...then validated_decompression_bomb_check() (src/PIL/Image.py:3586) raisesDecompressionBombError for anything above 2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS(178 956 970 px by default), but by then self._size already holds the rejectedvalue and nothing restores it: seek() (GifImagePlugin.py:166-179) only rollsback on EOFError, and _seek(0) only ever grows _size. The object that theapplication still holds therefore reports im.size == (40000, 40000) whileim.im is the 1×1 buffer of frame 0. Compare the two dispose-extent checks afew lines further down in the same function (GifImagePlugin.py:383 and :407),which call _decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size) before the correspondingImage.core.fill(), and TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare()(src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321), which checks _tile_size beforeallocating from it.With this 60-byte GIF (hex)47494638396101000100800000000000ffffff          GIF89a, 1x1 screen, 2-entry global palette2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00               frame 0: 1x1 @ (0,0), LZW data2c00000000409c409c00                            frame 1 descriptor: 40000x40000 @ (0,0)2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00               another 1x1 frame3b                                              trailerImage.open() succeeds (im.size == (1, 1)), im.seek(1) raisesDecompressionBombError: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels, and afterwards im.size == (40000, 40000),im.im.size == (1, 1), im.tell() == 0.What happens next depends on what the application does with the object, butseveral ordinary operations take their dimensions from im.size rather thanfrom the C buffer:Retrying im.seek(1). The failed _seek left self.__offset == 0 and thefile pointer just past the 9-byte descriptor, so the retry parses whateverfollows — in the file above, a valid 1×1 frame — and succeeds. im.load()then runs GifImageFile.load_prepare():# src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:452-456elif self.mode in ("RGB", "RGBA"):    self._prev_im = self.im    if self._frame_palette:        self.im = Image.core.fill("P", self.size, self._frame_transparency or 0)memsets a 40000×40000 "P" image (1.6 GB) to decode a1×1 tile into, and load_end() (GifImagePlugin.py:485-491) fills a sec

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit
items.summary: ============================================================================EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limitLocation: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:92  in Ghostscript()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================When an application opens an untrusted Encapsulated PostScript file and asks Pillow to render it at a larger scale, Pillow has Ghostscript produce an image several times bigger than Pillow's configured size limit allows. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file.The cause is in Ghostscript() in src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's scale (lines 93-94) and passes the product to gs as the -g output geometry. It never calls Image._decompression_bomb_check() on the scaled size. The only check is the one Image.open() ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and load(scale=2) then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. DecompressionBombError fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption.The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons:The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file.With the default warning filter, Image.open() already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at scale=1.Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since gs runs with no timeout.This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF load(dpi) gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing Image.open() and reaching gs with -g18000x18000. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included.DetailsEpsImageFile.load(scale=N) (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders width*N × height*N pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one Image.open() ran on the unscaled, file-declared width × height. The scaled product is never passed to Image._decompression_bomb_check() before gs is started.This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89,478,485), so Image.open() accepts it without even a warning:%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000%%EndComments0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto strokeshowpageim.load(scale=2) on it then executesgs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpagei.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS), whose pnmraw output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by Image.open() with DecompressionBombError before Ghostscript is ever run; via scale=2 the same raster is rendered first and the DecompressionBombError only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. (Between 1× and 2× MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, Image.open() only emits DecompressionBombWarning, so with the default warning filter an EPS declaring e.g. 13377×13377 is already rendered at scale=1 — a 537 MB PNM. Against that baseline, scale=2 is 4× an already-permitted render.)The arithmetic is in Ghostscript():# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:91-97    # Hack to support hi-res rendering    scale = int(scale) or 1    width = size[0] * scale    height = size[1] * scale    # resolution is dependent on bbox and size    res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0])    …# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:139-142    command = [        gs_binary,        "-q",  # quiet mode        f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",  # set output geometry (pixels)    …# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:165-168        subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)        with Image.open(outfile) as out_im:            out_im.load()            return out_im.im.copy()and its caller does nothing between taking scale from the application and invoking it:# src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:411-417    def load(self, scale: int = 1, transparency: bool = False) -> …:        # Load EPS via Ghostscript        if self.tile:            assert self.fp is not None            self.im = Ghostscript(self.tile, self.size, self.fp, scale, transparency)size here is self._size, computed in _open() from the file's %%Bound

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips
items.summary: ============================================================================TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG stripsLocation: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:554  in _decodeStrip()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================Pillow hands back leftover process memory as image pixels when it opens a small crafted TIFF file. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content.The bug is in _decodeStrip() in src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c, and _decodeTile() has the same shape. The function realloc()s state->buffer to TIFFStripSize() bytes without initialising it and calls TIFFReadEncodedStrip(). Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all RowsPerStrip rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early.The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with b"LEAK". It then finds 15,872 copies of LEAK in rows 8–255 of the decoded image (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs). Under glibc's MALLOC_PERTURB_, those rows are entirely the allocator's fill byte. A well-formed control file decodes correctly in both cases.This is a read of uninitialised heap memory, not memory corruption. Each strip can disclose up to width × RowsPerStrip bytes, and what comes back depends on the allocator's state at the time. The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", first released in Pillow 6.0.0). The tile path has had the same pattern since f0436a4ddc95 (Pillow 5.3.0).Detailssrc/libImaging/TiffDecode.c decodes compressed TIFFs through libtiff into a strip(or tile) buffer that it realloc()s to TIFFStripSize() bytes and never initialises, andthen copies all RowsPerStrip rows of that buffer into the image wheneverTIFFReadEncodedStrip() does not return -1. libtiff's JPEG codec does not fail when theJPEG stream inside a strip has fewer rows than the strip: it decodes the rows that existand returns the full strip size. The rows it did not write are whatever the heap heldbefore, and Pillow returns them as pixels.A 478-byte file shows it: a classic little-endian TIFF, 256×256, BitsPerSample=8,Compression=7, PhotometricInterpretation=1, RowsPerStrip=256, one strip whose datais a baseline JPEG of 256×8 pixels (as written by Image.new("L",(256,8),200).save(…,"JPEG")).Image.open(BytesIO(data)).load() succeeds with default settings (compressed TIFFs alwaystake the libtiff path). Rows 0–7 of the result are the JPEG content (value 200); theremaining 63488 bytes of im.tobytes() are heap garbage: run under glibc'sMALLOC_PERTURB_=1 they are all 0xFE, under MALLOC_PERTURB_=170 all 0x55 (thefresh-malloc fill byte), and in a process that has just freed buffers containingb"LEAK" they contain 15872 copies of LEAK.Feeding the same file to libtiff 4.5.0 directly confirms the library side:TIFFReadEncodedStrip(t, 0, buf, 65536) printsJPEGPreDecode: Warning, Improper JPEG strip/tile size, expected 256x256, got 256x8.,returns 65536, and leaves 63488 of the 65536 buffer bytes untouched. Pillow installsTIFFSetWarningHandler(NULL) (TiffDecode.c:682), so the warning is not visible either.The strip path:// src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:552    /* realloc to fit whole strip */    /* malloc check above */    new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);      // state->bytes = TIFFStripSize()    …    state->buffer = new_data;    for (; state->y < state->ysize; state->y += rows_per_strip) {        …            if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip(                    tiff,                    TIFFComputeStrip(tiff, state->y, plane),                    (tdata_t)state->buffer,                    strip_size                ) == -1) {                … return -1;            }            …            // iterate over each row in the strip and stuff data into image            for (strip_row = 0;                 strip_row < MIN((INT32)rows_per_strip, state->ysize - state->y);                 strip_row++) {                …                shuffler(                    (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff + strip_row] +                        state->xoff * im->pixelsize,                    state->buffer + strip_row * row_byte_size,                    state->xsiz

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: TIFF encoder ColorMap plane-size mismatch causes a heap out-of-bounds read
items.summary: SummaryA small attacker-supplied TIFF can be opened and loaded normally, then reach an out-of-bounds read when an application saves it back to TIFF with retained metadata. The fixed reproducer is a 1×1, 16-bit grayscale, PackBits-compressed TIFF containing tag 320 (ColorMap) with 768 SHORT values: three zero-filled planes of 256 entries each. No Python object is forged and no metadata is injected after loading.Pillow's TIFF encoder allocates 768 × 2 = 1536 bytes, then passes three plane pointers separated by 256 SHORT entries to libtiff. With BitsPerSample = 16, libtiff instead expects 65536 SHORT values per plane and attempts a 131072-byte read from a plane pointer. Existing ASAN observations identify a heap-buffer-overflow READ crossing the 1536-byte allocation made in PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew.The malformed ColorMap need not be a valid palette for this grayscale image. The issue is that accepted metadata is forwarded on save without reconciling the fixed plane extent with the effective sample depth. Opening/loading alone is not the demonstrated fault; the encoder path is required.Impact and prerequisitesAn application must accept the input, retain the relevant TIFF metadata, and invoke the libtiff-backed TIFF save path. The observed consequence is an out-of-bounds read and ASAN termination. Process-memory exposure during encoding is a potential consequence, not demonstrated by extracting arbitrary heap contents in this report. No arbitrary read primitive, full memory-disclosure chain, code execution, address-space bypass, or cross-process effect is claimed.The 131072-byte attempted copy is not the number of bytes proven disclosed. This report does not run a synthetic-canary serializer or collect an unsanitized encoded output.Tested environment and limits of the evidenceThe existing observations were recorded on August 30, 2026, with CPython 3.11.8 on macOS ARM64, using the unmodified official Pillow 12.3.0 wheel and its bundled libtiff 4.7.1:Wheel: pillow-12.3.0-cp311-cp311-macosx_11_0_arm64.whlWheel size: 4785266 bytesWheel SHA-256: 37d6d0a00072fd2948eb22bce7e1475f34569d90c87c59f7a2ec59541b77f7a6Pillow source revision: bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13dBundled libtiff SHA-256: e8988717b7470394a47d5ccd343130796b24ee70b6d885d3818e0e0b53238be1Apple's ASAN runtime was injected at process startup. This is not an ASAN-rebuilt Pillow wheel; allocation/memcpy interception detects the reported boundary violation, but the wheel's native instructions are not comprehensively instrumented.Only this concrete full-package environment is established here. No affected-version range, current development-branch result, or patched release is asserted. Severity is Unknown; no CVSS score is proposed.Separate earlier evidence reached the original Pillow 8.0.1 encoder constructor compiled as a component against a modern Python/libtiff environment. That was not a complete Pillow 8.0.1 installation and does not establish the historical package's full runtime behavior. It is not part of this reproducer or an affected-version range.Observed evidence and controlsThe earlier integration harness performed the natural sequence Image.open(BytesIO(input)), image.load(), then image.save(BytesIO(), format="TIFF"), without replacing the image's metadata. Each case was recorded three times:Original fixtureBytesRecorded resultcolormap161685Loaded as I;16; save terminated with ASAN exit 86, READ of size 131072 crossing a 1536-byte heap region (3/3).colormap81684Same fixed ColorMap, but 8-bit samples; save succeeded and retained SHORT/count 768 (3/3).colormap_absent137Same 16-bit geometry without ColorMap; save succeeded (3/3).Address-free summary of the recorded native diagnostic:AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflowREAD of size 1310720 bytes after 1536-byte regionCopy path: memcpy -> _TIFFmemcpy -> setByteArray -> _TIFFsetShortArrayExt           -> _TIFFVSetField -> TIFFVSetField -> ImagingLibTiffSetField           -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNewAllocation: calloc -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNewInput SHA-256 values (also enforced inside the script):colormap16: 5f38e0ead90b97949fb0c98c63f9c68d00ba9181db6631ecb8927376dcc75f4dcolormap8: fdb26d9135549ed44824901985086c5ee4f06515699ca3291e498c523935405ccolormap_absent: bd54979624f3ffb713342e0458caff9e17c477f940cda2f0960feebfabbc9556Root cause and source referencesPillow src/encode.c, lines 870–899, pinned revision: the ColorMap tuple must contain exactly 768 entries; a 1536-byte allocation is passed with a fixed stride of 256. items.title: [pillow] Pillow: Unbounded recursion parsing a PDF page tree or trailer chain (incomplete fix for CVE-2026-42310)
items.summary:
SummaryWhen an application appends to an existing PDF with Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True), Pillow parses that file with PdfParser. Two recursive parsers have no effective bound. linearize_page_tree follows /Kids with no visited set or depth limit, so a cyclic or duplicated page tree recurses without end. read_prev_trailer rejects only an exactly repeated /Prev offset, so a long chain of unique offsets still recurses. The trailer-loop guard added for CVE-2026-42310 does not cover either case.Detailslinearize_page_tree recurses on /Kids with no cycle or depth check:src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1078-1092read_prev_trailer catches only a repeated offset:src/PIL/PdfParser.py:697-720 (the processed_offsets check at :714-718 is the CVE-2026-42310 fix; a unique-offset chain slips past it)PoCfrom PIL import PdfParser# A page tree whose /Pages nodes reference each other in a cycle (2 -> 3 -> 2).objs = {    1: b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>",    2: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 >>",    3: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [2 0 R] /Count 1 >>",}buf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
")off = {}for oid in (1, 2, 3):    off[oid] = len(buf)    buf += b"%d 0 obj
" % oid + objs[oid] + b"
endobj
"xref = len(buf)buf += b"xref
0 4
0000000000 65535 f 
"buf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n 
" % off[o] for o in (1, 2, 3))buf += b"trailer
<< /Root 1 0 R /Size 4 >>
startxref
%d
%%%%EOF
" % xrefopen("poc.pdf", "wb").write(buf)PdfParser.PdfParser("poc.pdf", mode="r+b")   # append=True parses the existing file the same wayRun it:$ python 11_poc.pyRecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceededThe 315-byte file triggers the recursion on parse. A duplicated (non-cyclic) /Kids tree instead produces super-linear CPU and memory work, and a long unique-offset /Prev chain triggers the trailer-side recursion.ImpactA service that appends to user-supplied PDFs, for example a stamping or watermarking pipeline, can be driven into uncaught recursion or heavy CPU and memory use before any image is written. Follow-up to CVE-2026-42310. Since Pillow's policy discourages filing plain Python exceptions as denial of service, lead with the cyclic-tree case, which burns CPU and memory rather than only raising RecursionError. The fix is a visited set plus a depth limit in both parsers.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-p4wg-p73j-c528https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112895https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/e2ae7eacad6de68c37eb28b633a97bebacf2c5bfhttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4wg-p73j-c528

items.title: [pillow] Pillow tiled-TIFF decoder reads past tile buffer in copy4 (Unpack.c:1290)
items.summary: SummaryPillow's libImaging _decodeTile decoder, used to decode tiled TIFF images, allocates a per-tile buffer using realloc(state->buffer, TIFFTileSize(tiff)). After each TIFFReadTile it then iterates tile_y from 0 up to current_tile_length and calls the configured row unpacker (here copy4) with the source pointer state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size. When libtiff returns a tile_bytes_size smaller than the worst-case row_byte_size * tile_length, the inner stride-and-copy loop walks past the realloc'd region and copy4 performs a 1024-byte memcpy that reads up to (tile_length-1) * row_byte_size + row_byte_size bytes from a buffer sized only to tile_bytes_size. The supplied PoC TIFF triggers a 1024-byte over-read exactly 0 bytes past a 196608-byte allocation. An attacker who can convince a Pillow-using application to decode a crafted TIFF can trigger a process crash (DoS) and may cause adjacent heap memory to be copied into the decoded pixel buffer.DetailsPillow's TIFF decoder, when libtiff reports the file is tiled, takes the _decodeTile path. The function:Asks libtiff for TIFFTileSize(tiff) (the bytes-per-tile) and TIFFTileRowSize(tiff) (the bytes per row as stored by libtiff).Reallocates state->buffer to exactly tile_bytes_size.For each tile origin (x, y) and each plane, calls TIFFReadTile into state->buffer, then walks the tile row by row, calling the configured ImagingShuffler (here copy4) on each row's worth of source bytes.The validation done before the loop is:if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {    state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;    return -1;}This rejects oversized libtiff tiles, but it does not reject undersized ones — i.e. the case where libtiff returns a tile_bytes_size strictly less than row_byte_size * tile_length. The loop body, however, indexes into the buffer assuming the buffer is at least row_byte_size * tile_length bytes long.Vulnerable Code// src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:446-490 — _decodeTilenew_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);   // bytes = tile_bytes_sizeif (!new_data) { ... }state->buffer = new_data;for (y = state->yoff; y < state->ysize; y += tile_length) {    for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) {        ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane];        for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) {            if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { ... }            current_tile_width  = min((INT32)tile_width,  state->xsize - x);            current_tile_length = min((INT32)tile_length, state->ysize - y);            for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                shuffler(                    (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                    state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size,   // <-- OOB stride                    current_tile_width                );            }        }    }}// src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1288-1291 — copy4 (the crash site)static voidcopy4(UINT8 *out, const UINT8 *in, int pixels) {    /* RGBA, CMYK quadruples */    memcpy(out, in, 4 * pixels);   // <-- ASAN-detected READ here}The PoC's tile metadata yields tile_width = tile_length = 256, row_byte_size = 1024 (4 bytes/pixel × 256 pixels), and tile_bytes_size = 196608 (which is 256·256·3 = three-channel-byte storage). The realloc'd buffer is 196608 bytes. The unpacker iterates tile_y from 0 to 255 and for the highest rows the source pointer state->buffer + tile_y * 1024 already lies at or past offset 196608 — the very last row's memcpy(in=buffer+255·1024, 1024) reads 1024 bytes starting 260096 - 196608 = 63488 bytes past the allocation; ASAN flags the very first byte past the heap region (READ of size 1024 at … 0 bytes after 196608-byte region).The mismatch is real: libtiff's TIFFTileSize returns the packed per-tile storage (which depends on the file's photometric/separation layout — it can legitimately be smaller than row_byte_size × tile_length), while the inner loop strides as if the buffer always equals row_byte_size × tile_length.AttributionThis issue was found by Anthropic from using Claude to study security of open source projects, and I am from Ada Logics helping validate the found issues and report to maintainers. The data in this report has been reviewed manually.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-462x-pgg6-55fphttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112395https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/76869efdbbf2ad7dccd7536520fb61b7a00ab61ehttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-462x-pgg6-55fp

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels
items.summary: ============================================================================OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixelsLocation: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483  in _decodeTile()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================Pillow reads past the end of a heap buffer when decoding certain malformed compressed TIFF files, and copies the bytes it reads into the pixels of the image it returns. An attacker who can get an application to open and load an image file, for example by uploading it to a service that returns thumbnails, previews or converted images, gets back fragments of that process's heap memory, including pointer values. A slightly larger file instead crashes the process. No special settings are needed, and nothing is written out of bounds.The bug is in _decodeTile() and _decodeAsRGBA() in src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c. Both size their decode buffer from libtiff's view of the pixel layout (TIFFTileSize()/TIFFTileRowSize(), or img.width * 4). They then unpack each row with the unpacker that TiffImagePlugin._setup() chose from Pillow's own parse of the directory, and neither checks that the unpacker's input row fits inside the row libtiff produced. _decodeStrip() has exactly this check, added for OSS-Fuzz crash-0da0 in 8.2.0, but the tile and RGBA paths never got it.The two parsers can be made to disagree with a duplicated PhotometricInterpretation or BitsPerSample tag, because libtiff keeps the first occurrence and Pillow keeps the last. Pillow then unpacks 4 to 8 bytes per pixel from rows that libtiff filled with 1 to 4 bytes, so the last rows of each tile are read from beyond the buffer. The disclosed memory is a few tile rows past the buffer, and the attacker chooses the tile width. The amount does not grow with the number of tiles, because the buffer is reused for every tile.The tile half was introduced in 1c295bf43 (first released in 8.2.0). The RGBA half was introduced in eb8c1206d, the CVE-2020-35654 fix (8.1.0).The attached reproducer runs against an unmodified build. It writes three roughly 400-byte files that load without error, yet the last pixel rows of each change with glibc's malloc fill pattern and contain heap pointer bytes. A fourth file with a 65536x16 tile segfaults in copy4 ← _decodeTile (TiffDecode.c:483) in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer.Details_decodeTile() and _decodeAsRGBA() in src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c size state->buffer from what libtiff says it will produce (TIFFTileSize(), resp. img.width * 4), but unpack each row with the shuffler that TiffImagePlugin._setup() selected from Pillow's own parse of the IFD. Nothing in either function checks that the unpacker's input row (width * state->bits / 8 bytes) fits inside the row libtiff wrote. _decodeStrip() has exactly that check; the other two do not. Whenever the two IFD parsers disagree about the pixel layout — a tag with the wrong count or type that libtiff ignores but Pillow accepts, or a duplicated PhotometricInterpretation/BitsPerSample/SamplesPerPixel entry (libtiff keeps the first occurrence, ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() the last) — the unpacker reads past the end of the heap buffer and the bytes it reads become pixels of the returned image. Any Pillow rawmode wider than libtiff's actual sample layout works (RGBX, RGB;16N, RGBA;16N, I;32, F;32F, …); RGBA;16N (64 bits/pixel) against 1-bit libtiff data is the largest ratio, where every row after the first of each tile is read almost entirely from beyond the buffer.The ~400-byte TIFF tile_count2.tif generated by the reproducer — one 16x16 tile, BitsPerSample 8, SamplesPerPixel 1, Compression 8 (Adobe Deflate), and PhotometricInterpretation written as a SHORT with count 2 (6, 6) — is opened by Image.open() as mode RGB with libtiff rawmode RGBX, and load() succeeds on the stock build. Rows 13–15 of the result contain bytes that lie 16, 32 and 48 bytes past the 256-byte tile buffer: decoding the same file twice under MALLOC_PERTURB_=85 and =170 yields identical rows 0–12 and different bytes in rows 13–15 (aa vs 55, i.e. glibc's fill pattern). Under an ASan build of the extensions the same load() reports heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 64 in copy4 (src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1290) called from src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483, against the 256-byte region allocated at TiffDecode.c:448. The same layout with a single 65536x16 tile (4.5 KB file) makes the stock build SIGSEGV in copy4 ← _decodeTile reading an unmapped address in most runs (whether it faults depends on what is mapped after the 1 MiB buffer; a wider tile makes it reliable).Why the two parsers disagreelibtiff 4.5 rejects a PhotometricInterpretation entry whose count is not 1 (TIFFFetchNormalTag: Incorrect count for "PhotometricInterpretation"; tag ignored), so for this file TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, …) returns 0 and libtiff treats the data as one 8-bit sample per pixel: TIFFT

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in ImagingJpegDecode
items.summary: SummaryJpegImageFile.draft() — which Image.thumbnail() calls automatically — requests 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 scaled JPEG output and shrinks self._size and the tile extents to match, so _setimage() allocates a single-row decode buffer of ceil(W/s) samples. ImagingJpegDecode() sets cinfo.scale_num/scale_denom, calls jpeg_start_decompress(), and then reads scanlines into that buffer without ever comparing cinfo.output_width, cinfo.output_height or cinfo.out_color_components against state->xsize, state->ysize and state->bits.libjpeg-turbo 3.x decodes lossless (SOF3) JPEG, but hardwires lossless streams to no scaling — the requested scale_denom is silently discarded. It therefore returns full-width W-sample rows into a buffer sized for ceil(W/s). Each jpeg_read_scanlines() call writes (W - ceil(W/s)) x components bytes past the end of the heap allocation, and the overflowing bytes are the decoded pixel values, which are byte-exact for an 8-bit grayscale lossless image.The input is a standards-compliant JPEG, so Image.open(..., formats=["JPEG"]) does not prevent it. Pillow's Python SOF parser already accepts marker 0xFFC3 ("SOF3", "Spatial lossless") at 8-bit precision, so the file opens normally as a JPEG / mode L image at its full declared size.Affected codeAt e41083f383c9cd3db95de52564cc0b6452313d4a (main, 2026-08-29):src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c:224-262 — ImagingJpegDecode(); jpeg_start_decompress() at :240, jpeg_read_scanlines() at :252, with no geometry check between them.src/decode.c:222-231 — _setimage(); state->buffer = calloc(1, state->bytes) with state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8.src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:428-464 — JpegImageFile.draft(); computes s and shrinks _size, the tile extents and decoderconfig with no notion of lossless coding.src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:271 — 0xFFC3: ("SOF3", "Spatial lossless", SOF).// src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c            if (context->scale > 1) {                context->cinfo.scale_num = 1;                context->cinfo.scale_denom = context->scale;            }            ...        case 2:            if (!jpeg_start_decompress(&context->cinfo)) {                break;            }            state->state++;            /* fall through */        case 3:            ok = 1;            while (state->y < state->ysize) {                ok = jpeg_read_scanlines(&context->cinfo, &state->buffer, 1);Because state->ysize (ceil(H/s)) can never equal libjpeg's output_height when s >= 2, the decode always ends in an error after the rows have already been written: the caller sees an exception and gets no pixels back. The OSError is a consequence of the overflow, not the issue being reported.PrimitivePer scanline: a contiguous write of (W - ceil(W/s)) x c bytes immediately past a calloc(ceil(W/s) x c) block, where c = 1 for mode L and 4 for RGB (RGBX) and CMYK; repeated for ceil(H/s) rows over the same region. The buffer size class is chosen by the attacker through W, and for grayscale the overflowing content is an arbitrary attacker-chosen byte string.Measured in the reproducer below: 1200x1100 mode L, s=2 — a 600-byte allocation, 600 bytes written past it, ASan reporting the whole 1200-byte row write as one memcpy.Threshold: draft() must select s >= 2, i.e. W // requested_w >= 2 and H // requested_h >= 2. For thumbnail((256,256)) with the default reducing_gap=2.0 that means W, H >= 1024.ReproductionSelf-contained Docker reproducer (Ubuntu 24.04, clang 20, libjpeg-turbo 3.1.4 and Pillow both built from source with -fsanitize=address; Pillow checked out at ${TARGET_COMMIT}, default e41083f383c9cd3db95de52564cc0b6452313d4a). Save the three files below as Dockerfile, make_sof3.py and trigger.py in an empty directory, then:docker build -t pillow-sof3-oob . && docker run --rm pillow-sof3-oobmake_sof3.py is a self-contained encoder that emits a standards-compliant 8-bit grayscale lossless-Huffman JPEG (SOI / DHT / SOF3 P=8, Y=1100, X=1200, Nf=1 / SOS Ss=1 predictor 1, Se=0, Ah=Al=0 / entropy-coded row differences / EOI), whose rows carry a repeating marker pattern. trigger.py opens it and calls thumbnail(), whose implicit draft() picks s=2 and allocates a 600-byte row buffer.DockerfileFROM ubuntu:24.04ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractiveARG TARGET_COMMIT=e41083f383c9cd3db95de52564cc0b6452313d4aARG CLANG_VERSION=20ARG LIBJPEG_TURBO_TAG=3.1.4RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \        ca-certificates git make cmake nasm pkg-config libc6-dev gcc \        wget gnupg lsb-release software-properties-common \        python3 python3-dev python3-pip python3-venv zlib1g-dev \    && wget -qO /tmp/llvm.sh https://apt.llvm.org/llvm.sh && chmod +x /tmp/llvm.sh && /tmp/llvm.sh ${CLANG_VERSION} \    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends clang-${CLANG_VERSION} llvm-${CLANG_VERSION} libclang-rt-${CLANG_VERSION}-dev \    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*ENV CC=clang-20ENV CXX=clang++-20ENV CFLAGS="-g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -O1 -fsanitize=address"ENV CXXFLAGS="-g -fno-

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Absolute-form request targets can spoof Request.scheme
items.summary: SummaryAn attacker sending an absolute-form request can spoof the scheme used.ImpactIf user code depends on the Request.scheme attribute for anything security related, an attacker may be able to circumvent this logic, tricking the application into thinking a connection is encrypted when it is not, or vice versa.WorkaroundA WAF rule to reject absolute-form requests (legitimate requests should only use this form for proxies).Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-f9xw-jh8m-3mwqhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111748https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6d4e7b01f9b951aa084a75d7356e907d4ee80411https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f9xw-jh8m-3mwq

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Cookie from subdomain can remove Host-Only Scope from existing cookies
items.summary: SummaryA subdomain can remove the Host-Only flag from an existing cookie to a parent domain.ImpactA user accessing untrusted subdomains could see their Host-Only protections stripped from cookies. Given most usecases won't reflect these cookies to a browser, the impact is limited.Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-gx76-c99x-2c96https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111749https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6a07c171ef9f3be583e2907dcd1931372efca8d6https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gx76-c99x-2c96

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Connector pool exhaustion via Max-Age overflow
items.summary: SummaryAn overflow in Max-Age processing can skip closing a connection.ImpactAn attacker may be able to exhaust the connection pool temporarily, until garbage collection resolves the connections.Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-6cjc-53gc-5rqmhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111065https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/9dd8eaf4e31f1237ef2c1574a8c82a739fca5805https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6cjc-53gc-5rqm

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Pure-Python parser request smuggling
items.summary: SummaryThe pure Python parser is vulnerable to an HTTP request smuggling attack.ImpactIf users are using the Python parser (AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS, or not a standard wheel installed), then an application may be vulnerable to a request smuggling attack.WorkaroundSwitch to the default C parser.Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-pqxq-w44r-73xwhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111750https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/9b27347e61454d9f8ca2055f4c67a37dee336e83https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pqxq-w44r-73xw

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: File descriptor exhaustion in multipart requests
items.summary: SummaryAn attacker can exhaust file descriptors with specially crafted multipart requests.ImpactIf a handler uses Request.post(), it may be possible for an attacker to use an unlimited number of file descriptors, potentially resulting in resource exhaustion.Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-9xw5-w5jj-pvcghttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111066https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/2d94633b7f1b4c1ba07d647b629a8440652b2d09https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9xw5-w5jj-pvcg
